spoken: Look up on a clear day, and the whole sky glows blue.
That's strange, when you think about it, because sunlight is white and the air looks perfectly clear.
So where does all that blue come from?
And once you know, there's a second puzzle. Why isn't the sky violet?
Violet? Nobody expects a violet sky.
No, but the physics of scattering points that way, and that's the fun part.
To get there, we need a tube of smoke, a fourth power, the sunsets of Mars, and your own eyes.
This is why the sky is blue.
Let's start with sunlight. It looks white, but it's a mixture of every colour of the rainbow.
Isaac Newton showed that with a prism, which spreads white light out into a spectrum.
So the colours were in there all along. The prism just sorts them out.
And light is a wave, so each colour has its own wavelength, which is the distance from one crest to the next.
How long are we talking?
Tiny. Red light has waves about 720 nanometres long, and violet about 380.
A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.
Right. And in between come orange, yellow, green and blue.
We'll keep comparing blue light at four hundred and fifty nanometres with red light at seven hundred.
Blue waves are shorter, and the whole story turns on that one difference.
People have wondered about the colour of the sky for centuries.
In the early fifteen-hundreds, Leonardo da Vinci guessed that sunlight scattered by tiny particles in the air makes the sky blue.
It was a good guess, but still only a guess.
The first steps toward a real explanation came in eighteen sixty-nine, from the Irish physicist John Tyndall.
He needed perfectly clean air for his work on heat, so he hunted for dust by shining bright light through it.
Then he slowly filled a tube with smoke, shone a beam along it, and saw something striking.
From the side, the beam looked blue. From the far end, it looked red.
It's the same beam, with two different colours, depending on where you look from.
The particles were scattering blue light out sideways, and letting the redder light carry straight on.
And Tyndall suggested that this is why the sky is blue.
So was he right?
Partly. But he couldn't explain why blue scatters more, and dust alone couldn't explain how intense the sky's blue is.
The explanation began in eighteen seventy-one, with a young British physicist called John William Strutt.
Two years later he became Lord Rayleigh, which is why the effect is called Rayleigh scattering.
So what actually happens when light meets a tiny particle?
Light is an electric and magnetic wave, and as it passes a particle, its electric field shakes the charges inside.
So the shaken particle turns into a tiny antenna, and sends out light of its own in new directions.
Exactly. And that works for particles far smaller than the wavelength, meaning less than about a tenth of it.
Then comes the key rule, that the scattering goes as one over the wavelength to the fourth power.
The fourth power. That's what makes it so lopsided.
Right. Halve the wavelength, and the scattering gets sixteen times stronger.
So take blue at 450 nanometres and red at 700. The ratio of 700 to 450, raised to the fourth power, is about 5.9.
So air scatters blue light nearly six times more strongly than red.
That's a big effect from a fairly modest difference in wavelength.
Then in eighteen ninety-nine, Rayleigh showed that the same rule applies to single molecules.
And molecules of nitrogen and oxygen are less than a nanometre across, which is hundreds of times smaller than a wave of light.
So the air itself scatters the light. No dust is needed.
That answers Tyndall's problem with the dust.
And later, Albert Einstein worked out the scattering by molecules in detail, and his result agreed with experiment.
So now picture sunlight streaming down through the air.
Most of it comes straight through, but some is scattered by molecules on the way.
And because short waves scatter most, it's mostly blue light that gets knocked off in new directions.
That scattered blue reaches your eyes from every part of the sky, so the whole dome glows.
And the Sun itself?
The light that comes straight through has lost a little blue, so the Sun looks slightly yellow.
Measure the light of a blue sky, and it holds every colour, with a broad peak between 450 and 485 nanometres.
So it holds every colour, not just blue.
Right, and our eyes take that mix as blue blended with white, which gives the soft colour we call sky blue.
You sometimes hear that the sky is blue because it reflects the sea. It's the other way round.
Seen from the beach, the sea looks blue partly because it reflects the sky.
Now let's go back to the puzzle from the start. Violet light has even shorter waves than blue.
At 400 nanometres, violet scatters more than 9 times as strongly as red.
So why isn't the sky violet?
There isn't one single reason. It takes a few things together.
Part of it is that sunlight holds less violet than blue to begin with.
And some of the violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, before it reaches us.
Still, a rainbow shows that plenty of violet gets through. So the rest of the answer is in our eyes.
For one thing, our eyes are less sensitive to violet.
And we see colour with three kinds of cone cells, which respond most strongly to red, green and blue light.
Skylight stimulates the red and green cones about equally, and the blue cones more strongly.
And our vision reads that combination as a pale blue.
So the colour isn't only out there in the sky.
No. The blue of the sky is partly physics, and partly the way we see.
Here's another one. If air turns sunlight blue, why are clouds white?
Clouds are made of water droplets, typically a few micrometres, or thousandths of a millimetre, across.
That still sounds tiny.
It is, but it's thousands of times bigger than an air molecule, and bigger than a wave of light.
And particles that big don't follow Rayleigh's rule. They scatter all colours about equally.
That's called Mee scattering, after the German physicist Gustav Mee.
And if you scatter every colour alike, white light stays white.
A thick cloud reflects seventy to ninety-five percent of the light that falls on it, across all colours.
That's why the tops of big clouds look so bright.
And the base can look grey, simply because less light makes it through.
The same kind of scattering makes haze look whitish, and puts a bright white glow around the Sun.
Scattered skylight has another property that our eyes can't see. It's polarised.
Polarised meaning what, exactly?
Light waves can vibrate in any direction across their path. In polarised light, one direction wins out.
And skylight is most strongly polarised in a band 90 degrees away from the Sun.
There, in a clear sky, the polarisation can reach about eighty percent.
Polarising sunglasses can make that part of the sky look a deeper blue.
Rayleigh's first papers on the sky, in eighteen seventy-one, were even titled On the light from the sky, its polarization and colour.
So the polarisation was part of the puzzle from the very start.
And many insects can sense this pattern and use it as a compass.
The idea goes back to Karl von Frisch's studies of honeybees.
From the pattern alone, an animal can work out where the Sun is, even when it's out of sight.
It's like a compass painted across the whole sky.
It has even been suggested that Viking sailors did something similar, with a crystal called a sunstone.
As the day ends, the same rule paints the sky in different colours.
When the Sun is high, its light takes the shortest route through the air.
Squeeze all the air above you to sea-level density, and it would be only about 8 kilometres deep.
Only eight kilometres? That's a thin blanket.
But near the horizon, sunlight has to slant through far more air, about 38 times as much.
That's like crossing more than three hundred kilometres of air at sea level.
And along that path, the blue and green are scattered out almost completely.
So what's left to reach you is orange and red.
That reddened light falls on clouds, and they scatter it back to us, painting red and orange on white.
So the clouds are still white. They're just lit by reddened light.
In very clear air, a setting Sun looks yellow.
Fine particles of smoke or dust make it redder, and sea salt can turn it orange.
And after sunset, ozone high in the atmosphere helps keep the sky overhead blue.
On other worlds, the physics is the same, but the air is different.
At the surface of Mars, the air is only 1 to 2 percent as dense as ours, and full of fine dust.
By day, the Martian sky is a butterscotch colour.
And at sunset?
Near the setting Sun, the Martian sky turns blue.
Blue sunsets, on the red planet?
Really. NASA's Curiosity rover photographed one in twenty fifteen, from Gale Crater.
According to NASA, the fine dust lets blue light through more efficiently than redder colours.
So the blue stays close to the Sun, while yellow and red light spreads across the sky.
It's the opposite of what happens on Earth.
So, why is the sky blue?
Sunlight holds every colour, and the molecules of the air scatter short waves far more than long ones.
Blue scatters nearly six times more than red, so scattered blue reaches us from all over the sky.
Violet scatters even more, but sunlight holds less of it, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
At sunset, the light crosses so much air that the blue is scattered away, leaving orange and red.
And clouds, made of far bigger droplets, scatter every colour alike, so they stay white.
That's a lot of sky to explain with one small rule.
Every patch of blue you see is sunlight that the air itself has turned toward your eyes.
